decision.ambiguity_note: Several class boundaries are inherently ambiguous in H&E histopathology: 'debris' vs 'background' vs 'mucus' overlap in appearance; 'cancer-associated stroma' vs 'smooth muscle' can be indistinguishable at the patch level; 'normal colon mucosa' vs early 'colorectal adenocarcinoma epithelium' involves a dysplastic continuum. The test set (CRC-VAL-7K) originates from a different clinical center, introducing uncontrolled variation in staining protocol, scanner calibration, and tissue preparation that can shift the visual appearance of every class, compounding label ambiguity. The test prevalence,
risks: Cross-institutional domain shift: test images from a different clinical center introduce uncontrolled staining, scanner, and tissue-preparation variability that is not captured by train/val splits.

Severe class-prevalence shift in test: 'adipose' prevalence nearly doubles (10.4%→18.6%, ratio 1.79) while 'debris' nearly halves (11.5%→4.7%, ratio 0.41), violating the i.i.d. assumption and biasing accuracy metrics.
Small per-class test counts (debris n=339, stroma n=421, smooth muscle n=592) yield high variance in per-class accuracy and make confidence intervals wide.
Label ambiguity between 'debris', 'background', and 'mucus' is exacerbated by inter-center staining differences, increasing misclassification risk that is not a model failure but a definitional one.
'Cancer-associated stroma' vs 'smooth muscle' boundary is patch-level ambiguous; inter-center variation in section thickness and fixation can shift which label a pathologist assigns.
Test-to-train prevalence ratios span 0.41–1.79, meaning a model trained on the train distribution will face a shifted prior at test time, inflating apparent error for under-represented test classes.
The 1.63× train imbalance is mild, but the effective test imbalance (adipose:debris ≈ 4:1) is substantially higher, so overall accuracy in the test set is dominated by adipose and mucus predictions.

No information on whether the 9-class taxonomy was applied identically across centers; a single pathologist vs. multi-reader labeling protocol difference would introduce systematic label noise in the test set.

decision.rationale: Channel means (0.74, 0.53, 0.71) are far from zero and stds (0.12–0.18) are small, so zero-centering and unit-variance scaling (standardize) gives the network a well-conditioned input distribution and accelerates convergence versus raw unit-range values. All three geometric augmentations (hflip, vflip, rotate90) are orientation-safe for tissue-type labels: histological structures such as glands, stroma, and necrosis are recognizable regardless of flip or 90° rotation. Applying them train-only (design_evidence=train_only) expands the effective training set by up to 8×, which is especially useful given the moderate class imbalance (ratio 1.63) and the smallest class at ~7.9 k samples, improving generalization without leaking test-time geometry.

decision.analysis: No prior validation results, so round 1 should establish a strong standardize-normalized baseline and a simpler diverse baseline. PathMNIST has 3 channels with non-uniform means/stds, so standardization is preferred. Class imbalance is mild (1.63), so one candidate uses class weighting and light label smoothing, while the other tests whether a plain loss with SGD and plateau scheduling is competitive. Weight decay is kept small to avoid over-regularization.

candidates.rationale: Residual CNN with moderate capacity, standardization, AdamW, cosine decay, mild class weighting and label smoothing for mild imbalance; hflip/vflip add spatial robustness without assuming orientation invariance.

Simpler tiny CNN baseline with SGD, plateau scheduling, larger batch, and no class weighting to test whether mild imbalance can be handled by standard loss; lower weight decay avoids excessive regularization.

decision.analysis: Round 1 clearly established that residual_cnn with adamw/cosine/class_weighting/standardize/hflip+vflip dominates (95.9% acc vs 73.6% for tiny_cnn+SGD). The winning config uses hidden=32, depth=3, dropout=0.2, lr=3e-4, wd=1e-4. For round 2 I will (1) widen the residual CNN to hidden=48 with slightly more dropout to test whether extra capacity at the same depth improves generalization, and (2) switch to the deeper resnet18 family at depth=4 with a marginally lower lr to probe whether a richer backbone helps on this 9-class pathology task. Both retain the proven optimizer/scheduler/normalization/augmentation recipe and keep weight decay minimal.

candidates.rationale: Widens the proven residual_cnn from hidden=32 to 48 at the same depth=3, with a small dropout bump to 0.25 to regularize the extra parameters. All other hyperparameters (adamw, cosine, lr=3e-4, wd=1e-4, class_weighting, label_smoothing=0.05, hflip+vflip, standardize) are held at the round-1 optimum to isolate the capacity effect.

Explores the resnet18 backbone at maximum depth=4 to test whether a richer residual architecture captures finer-grained pathology patterns. lr lowered to 2e-4 for the deeper network's stability. Retains the winning adamw/cosine/class_weighting/standardize/hflip+vflip recipe and minimal weight decay.
